title: MLB’s Garbage Time is Getting Out of Control
subtitle: Nearly 1 percent of all runs are allowed by non-pitchers now.
contentHtml:
Friday night’s 20-0 (!) Milwaukee Brewers rout over the Cincinnati Reds offered a sight that has become all too common across baseball in recent seasons, and especially this year: A position-player (Jose Trevino) on the mound, lobbing a 32-mph Eephus pitch to a fellow batter (William Contreras) who absolutely smokes it into the left-field bleachers for a home run:

Trevino is the king of this: He leads all non-pitchers in runs allowed this season at 15, which is only 2 shy of Javier Sanoja’s divisional-era MLB single-season record of 17 (set last year). His career ERA is 12.83 in 11 appearances — all to “close out” games — and he’s allowed home runs to 6.1 percent of the batters he’s faced this year. The average Leverage Index in his pitching appearances is, unsurprisingly, 0.00. He is the definition of the mop-up, garbage-time position-player that you throw on the mound and let absorb a bunch of meaningless runs to finish off a blowout.

But Trevino is hardly alone in that role — and it’s one that is coming up more and more often.

Subscribe now

Position players account for 0.36 percent of all innings pitched this year, which sounds tiny — but that’s not only the all-time MLB record in a single season, but it is roughly double what the figure was just five years ago (0.19 percent in 2021) and 6.3 times what it was a decade ago. As recently as 2006, zero innings were mopped up by position players, but now it has become standard strategy to have them save the real bullpen by eating up those garbage innings late in laughers.

Position-player pitching keeps rising

The volume of those laughers is certainly increasing as well. The average margin deciding an MLB game (3.58 runs) is tracking to be eighth-highest in any season since 1970, but the real pattern is in the tail of the distribution — 2026 sees the sixth-highest modern share of games decided by 10+ runs (4.51 percent), fifth-highest share of games decided by 15+ runs (0.59 percent) and the very highest share of games decided by at least 20 runs (0.18 percent), like Friday’s Brewers-Reds contest.

MLB blowouts are getting crazier

And these two factors have now formed a feedback loop of sorts, where margins are more likely to get out of hand, causing teams to put non-pitchers on the mound… which then causes the score to get even more out of hand, and so forth.

When the score margin was in double-digits at a given moment, ERA used to be higher than normal — but not too much so. From 1974-2017, the average leaguewide ERA was 4.11, which rose to 4.50 with a 10+ run margin at the time of the pitch, and 4.55 with a 15+ run margin. (OPS was affected even less — .732 under all situations, .741 with a margin of 10+, .742 when it got to 15+.) But since 2018, those figures have ballooned massively, from a 4.21 ERA and .726 OPS across all situations to 5.18/.792 when the margin is 10+ and 6.37/.864 when it gets to 15+.

Offenses explode in garbage time recently

This trend can be directly traced to the trend of having those scenarios be handled increasingly by non-pitchers. In situations where the margin is 10+ runs but there’s still a “real” pitcher in the game, OPS allowed is still .736 this season, fairly comparable to the .719 mark allowed by all pitchers in all scenarios. But with a position-player on the mound — something that used to be reserved just for the trailing team, but now also includes the leader as well1 — OPS allowed rises to 1.178, or nearly 460 (!) points higher than in a normal situation.

Because of all this, the share of all runs in MLB allowed by non-pitchers has risen far more sharply than even the share of innings they pitch:

Position players now allow nearly 1% of all MLB runs

The two figures used to track fairly close together, in part a product of how seldom position players were used to pitch at all before the 2010s. But now, their usage is way up and they are soaking up a hugely disproportionate share of all opposing damage done by batters.

MLB saw this trend rising just a few years ago, instituting a rule that position players can only pitch if either his team was trailing by at least eight runs (at any point), if his team is winning by at least 10 runs in ninth inning, or if the game is in extra innings. But that rule didn’t do much to curtail the proliferation of non-pitchers pitching, since it merely “restricted” their use to the exact kinds of extreme blowouts that have themselves become increasingly common (and feed further off, you know, non-pitchers pitching).

Why does any of this matter? After all, the trend does do its intended job of preserving “real” pitching arms for innings that actually have leverage value, which you can’t necessarily fault teams for trying to do. And it doesn’t really affect the overall outcomes of games, since a double-digit margin comeback in the ninth inning has never happened before. (Also, no position-player has ever blown a save since that stat began being tracked in 1969, as far as I can tell.)

One tangible way it warps the game is through inflating opponent batting statistics — which is cute when it happens in limited doses, but less so when nearly 1 percent of all runs in the league are scored in non-competitive, non-representative situations. The Cubs have scored a league-high 26 runs off of non-pitchers, which is more than 3 percent of their league-leading total overall. (Joining them in scoring double-digit runs off non-pitchers are the Rockies, Brewers, Pirates and Braves.) Seven of Chicago’s 204 home runs (or 3.4 percent) have been off non-pitchers.

This isn’t to pick on the Cubs; they’re the league’s most explosive hitting team off of everyone, real pitchers and fake ones alike. But the game becomes a farce, both in terms of its records and its competitive quality, when — instead of the best in the world — players are on the field who deliberately aren’t qualified for what they’re trying to do. Garbage time is inevitable in sports — in the NBA, nearly 10 percent of star players’ scoring is done in notably low-leverage moments. But at least that’s still a version of basketball, not the beer-league softball these Eephus-fests start to resemble.

At a certain point, Major League Baseball should ask whether it is comfortable with an increasing share of its product consisting of something other than, well, major-league baseball.
